title: Transformers Converge to Invariant Algorithmic Cores
claim: Independently trained models differ in weights and geometry yet converge on functionally equivalent, statistically aligned and necessary-and-sufficient low-dimensional cores.
layout: 5 panels in one row, A–E; shared heatmap colorbars, unit-circle plot at right
description: A single-row figure with five labeled panels (A–E) of quantitative plots. A, B and C pair a red-blue diverging colormap with annotated numbers. A is a 3×3 heatmap of full-model weight cosine similarity: the diagonal is 1.00 and the off-diagonals are near 0.03–0.05, shown in dark blue. B is a bar chart of test accuracy. Gray control bars (Optimal, Full model, Chance) sit beside blue ablation bars (Core+, Core−). Core+ is high and Core− is low, with error bars. C is a 3×3 heatmap of core projector overlap, again near zero off the diagonal. D is a 3×3 heatmap of mean CCA between cores, all red at 0.97–0.99. E is a unit circle in the complex plane. Blue ground-truth eigenvalue dots are overlaid with red × marks inferred from the core. The contrast between the blue heatmaps in A and C and the red heatmap in D draws the eye first.
caption: Transformers trained on the same Markov task converge to a shared 3D causal core. Three one-layer transformers were trained with different random seeds on next-token prediction for a four-state Markov chain (Appendix [ref]). (A) Learned weights differ substantially across runs measured by cosine similarity. (B) 3D cores extracted from each 64D hidden state are necessary and sufficient under ablation (\tabl{tab:mark_ablations}), and compared to optimal $\sum_i \pi_i \max_j T_{ij}$ and chance $\max (\sta)$ theoretical controls, with transition matrix $\mar$ and stationary distribution $\sta$; points show individual accuracies and bars denote mean$\pm$sem. (C) Cores geometrically diverge with projector overlaps near zero and principal angles nearly orthogonal (\tabl{tab:mark_cca}). (D) Cores statistically align with mean cross-core CCAs reaching near unity (also see \tabl{tab:mark_cca}). (E) Dynamics fit in core recover the Markov chain nontrivial spectrum (\tabl{tab:mark_spec}).
abstract: Training selects for behavior, not circuitry: many weight configurations can implement the same function. Studying any single trained neural network thus risks describing accidents of one training run rather than the computation itself. This work shifts focus from what transformers happen to do to what they must do by extracting algorithmic cores, compact subspaces that are necessary and sufficient for a task and that recur across independently trained models. Here, Algorithmic Core Extraction (ACE) is introduced to isolate these subspaces, causally validate them, and recover the algorithms they implement, from synthetic tasks to large pretrained models. Markov-chain transformers embed 3D cores in nearly orthogonal subspaces yet recover identical transition spectra. Modular-addition transformers form compact cyclic cores at grokking that later inflate under continued regularization, redundantly distributing the same computation across many functionally equivalent modes. This functional redundancy accelerates the transition from memorization to generalization, yielding an inverse scaling law for grokking time. In six language models spanning two orders of magnitude in scale (GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large, LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2, and Qwen2.5), subject-verb agreement is governed by a single, steerable axis that aligns across architectures. Flipping this axis inverts grammatical number throughout open-ended generation. For indirect object identification, a multi-step task, the same six models route computation through compact multi-dimensional cores at two sites, linked by a linear operator that transfers across model families. Together these results suggest that beneath the apparent complexity of trained transformers lies a simpler, shared computational structure, and that targeting invariants rather than parameterizations may offer a more tractable path to mechanistic understanding and control.
